prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are a new organising principle for electronic phases, classified by topology rather than broken symmetry, and the discovery has the theory-to-experiment arc that I trust most: Kane and Mele predicted the Z2 state and the quantum spin Hall effect, and Molenkamp's group observed protected edge transport in HgTe/CdTe wells. The picture has been confirmed for almost two decades by independent transport, ARPES and STM work across many materials, and band-structure calculations can reproduce the surface and edge spectra quantitatively. It is not a premature or technology-driven choice. The field has spread into topological photonics, magnetism and superconductivity, and it is the one candidate on the shortlist that six of eight members ranked and five placed in their top three, so it is where the committee's judgements converge most. The prize would also say something true about quantum mechanics still producing surprises in ordinary band insulators.
statement.case_against: The credited trio does not cover the full history. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal pointed Molenkamp to HgTe, Zhang died in 2018, and the 3D case (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan's ARPES) is outside the names we may use, so the citation has to be worded narrowly around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and a three-person prize leaves a visible fairness gap. The quantisation in HgTe is also imperfect in long edges, and practical impact is still limited. Finally, our own preference as condensed-matter physicists may inflate this candidate relative to atomic-physics and astrophysics cases that we are less able to judge.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B018 first alongside me and treats Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a clean three-person configuration, while flagging that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work are not credited and that the later quantum anomalous Hall experiments are a separate discovery.
responses.response: I agree on the configuration and on keeping the quantum anomalous Hall effect out of this citation; it is a distinct experimental discovery and mixing them would blur the citation. Where I would go further than your note is that the omission is not just a historical footnote. The committee should word the citation around the prediction of the Z2 state and the quantum spin Hall effect and the HgTe observation, so it does not claim the whole of topological matter. I do not think the BHZ gap is disqualifying, because the Nobel statutes limit us to three and the decisive theoretical step for time-reversal-invariant systems was Kane and Mele.

responses.point: Mehlig put fluctuation theorems first and B018 second, and he stresses that B032 is simple, universal, rigorously provable and overdue, with only Jarzynski, Evans and Seifert as the most defensible trio.
responses.response: I respect the elegance of exact fluctuation relations and I think the maturity case is fair, but I would qualify it. Much of the experimental testing (RNA pulling, colloids) is a confirmation of an exact theorem, so nature has not surprised us, and the priority chain among Evans, Gallavotti-Cohen, Jarzynski, Crooks and Kurchan is exactly the sort of attribution dispute that a three-person cap handles badly. I also cannot judge statistical physics as well as the committee's other members. I would welcome hearing how you rank B032 against B018 on discovery content rather than on the generality of the result, and I do not see it as an obstacle that the topological case is also incomplete on credit, since the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp core is more clearly separable.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the optical lattice clock first and says the Katori-Ye credit is clean, strongly confirmed across Sr, Yb and Hg laboratories, and timely, while placing topological insulators fourth and deferring to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: Your credit and maturity arguments for B041 are convincing and I take them seriously; it is the best-attributed candidate on the list and I list it as an alternative. My reservation is about the discovery content, which you and Kroll also raised as the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes. The fundamental-physics payoffs so far are constraints, not discoveries, so the case rests mostly on metrology. Because you defer to us on how central the quantum spin Hall effect is relative to the 3D materials, I will say plainly that I regard the 2D effect as the cleaner, separable discovery and that its independent confirmation is at least as extensive as for the clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first, calling it a clean device discovery, a natural continuation of the 2025 circuit line, and timely, while openly flagging his own programme ties and that he would defer on the final configuration.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about the conflict of interest. I have two concerns about B020 as a first choice. First, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes a second circuit prize so soon hard to justify, and Kroll made the same point. Second, the four-name credit, with Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff all strong, makes the allocation harder than for B018. If the committee does want a quantum-technology prize, I would prefer that it be separated clearly from 2025, but I do not think it should displace a topological-matter prize that has had no recognition.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B018 third and B030 fourth, praising the Kane-Mele prediction as the pattern of a theory prediction that nature confirmed, and noted that B030 may be early because the discovery is under a decade old and the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with your pattern and your assessment of B030, which I ranked second. The reproducibility is broad but twist-angle disorder and strain make device-to-device variability large, and the interpretation of the superconductivity is not settled, so I would keep it as a strong alternative for a later cycle rather than this one. Where I differ slightly from your trio is that I would credit MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero if the committee does choose it, since Bistritzer's separate share is hard to defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect, given that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D topological insulator work are outside the credited names.
Whether the fundamental-physics payoff and attribution of B041 are stronger than I judge, since atomic physics is outside my core expertise.
Whether B030 should wait for a settled understanding of the superconducting pairing mechanism, or whether broad reproduction is enough.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: I have no stated personal, supervisory or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori or Ye. My Wallenberg and Uppsala funding and my theory work on magnetism and spectra are general background and not a tie to any shortlisted candidate.
